cards.term: Ch. 10: Key component of a truly national market economy?
cards.def: An efficient transportation system. The book says that to become truly national, a market economy needed an efficient transportation network linking the regions.

cards.term: Ch. 10: Most expansive economic force in the quarter-century after the War of 1812?
cards.def: Cotton production. The cotton trade was the major expansive force in the economy until the depression of 1839.

cards.term: Ch. 10: What did the Erie Canal stimulate after it paid for itself?
cards.def: Construction of other canals by other cities and states. Philadelphia, Baltimore, Ohio, and Indiana rushed to build their own after New York's success.

cards.term: Ch. 10: Steamboat: first introduced / greatest impact?
cards.def: On the Hudson River; on western rivers. Fulton's Clermont ran from New York City to Albany in 1807, but steamboats had their greatest effect on western rivers.

cards.term: Ch. 10: Marshall Court promoted enterprise by... (3 ways)
cards.def: Upholding private contracts; blocking state interference with private property; and increasing Congress's power over interstate commerce. (EXCEPT: it did not turn Native American lands over to eastern developers.)

cards.term: Ch. 10: Lowell workforce before 1845?
cards.def: Young women. The mills first hired daughters of New England farm families; only after 1845 did Irish immigrants become a large share of the workforce.

cards.term: Ch. 10: National market economy did all of these EXCEPT...?
cards.def: It did not significantly elevate the status of workers. It did raise per capita wealth, stimulate materialism, and push society toward greater specialization, but even well-paid workers sensed a decline in status.

cards.term: Ch. 10: Why anxiety amid early-nineteenth-century prosperity?
cards.def: Cyclical depressions made that prosperity seem fleeting. Boom-and-bust cycles (1819, 1837, 1839-1843) left Americans optimistic but insecure.

cards.term: Ch. 10: What did the factory system ask of workers?
cards.def: To forgo the traditional artisan system of mentorship for industrial productivity. Factories replaced the close master-apprentice bond with clock discipline and a sharp split from management.

cards.term: Ch. 10: Key to making the Merrimack valley the nation's greatest industrial center?
cards.def: Regulating the river's waters. By controlling the Merrimack with canals, dams, and New Hampshire lakes, the Boston Associates made the valley the country's greatest industrial center.

cards.term: Ch. 10: Where did the Erie Canal actually run?
cards.def: Albany on the Hudson River to Buffalo on Lake Erie (364 miles, built 1818-1825). It did not connect the Hudson to the Ohio River, and it paid for itself within a few years.

cards.term: Ch. 10: Lowell after 1845: what changed in the workforce?
cards.def: A shift from native-born farm daughters to Irish immigrants. The Irish were only 8 percent of Lowell's workforce in 1845, but almost half by 1860, and wages fell.

cards.term: Ch. 11: To reconcile equality and opportunity, Americans committed to...?
cards.def: Equality of opportunity. They rejected equality of condition; the book says every man should have an equal chance to become as unequal as he can.

cards.term: Ch. 11: As president, John Quincy Adams...?
cards.def: Proposed a broad program of support for manufacturing, agriculture, and the arts. His plans for federal promotion of manufacturing, agriculture, arts, literature, and science alarmed opponents.

cards.term: Ch. 11: Why did political involvement grow after 1820?
cards.def: A growing conviction that government should promote the economic well-being of society. After the market revolution and the Panic of 1819, Americans held government responsible for relieving distress and promoting prosperity.

cards.term: Ch. 11: How did Jackson view the spoils system?
cards.def: He defended it as a democratic reform. He treated rotation in office as a way to keep bureaucrats from becoming entrenched; he did not invent the practice.

cards.term: Ch. 11: Free Blacks in the North during the Jacksonian era...?
cards.def: Increasingly emphasized racial unity, self-help, and a renewal of ties with Africa. They founded schools, churches, and mutual-aid societies, and some supported emigration to Africa, even as militants like David Walker later denounced colonization.

cards.term: Ch. 11: How did Webster refute Calhoun's theory of government?
cards.def: The Constitution was created by "the people," not as a compact among the separate states. Webster called it "the people's constitution, the people's government, made for the people, made by the people, and answerable to the people."

cards.term: Ch. 11: How did Jackson finally destroy the national bank?
cards.def: By removing federal funds from it and depositing them in selected state banks ("pet banks"). After vetoing recharter, he had Roger Taney shift the deposits; the Bank's charter then expired in 1836.

cards.term: Ch. 11: What would you expect of the Whigs in the 1830s-1840s?
cards.def: Support for federal intervention to promote national economic development. Whigs wanted an active, well-regulated government that used its power to protect rights and guarantee opportunity.

cards.term: Ch. 11: Most popular entertainment in Jacksonian America?
cards.def: The minstrel show. In the 1830s-40s, white actors in blackface made minstrel shows the most popular entertainment in northern cities.

cards.term: Ch. 11: In the Jacksonian party system, who wanted active government?
cards.def: The Whigs supported a very active role for government; the Democrats generally favored limited government. Whigs were comfortable with the market; Democrats were uneasy about it.

cards.term: Ch. 11: Did Jackson create the spoils system?
cards.def: No. It was already a traditional practice; he defended using it as a democratic reform called rotation in office.

cards.term: Ch. 12: Who founded modern revivalism?
cards.def: Charles Grandison Finney. The book calls him the founder of modern revivalism and the man who embodied the new evangelicalism.

cards.term: Ch. 12: The ideal of domesticity held that...?
cards.def: Women's sphere was the home and family. The cult of domesticity taught that men belonged in business and politics while women ruled the domestic sphere.

cards.term: Ch. 12: Most important new Black independent church?
cards.def: The African Methodist Episcopal Church. Organized at Philadelphia in 1816, with Richard Allen as its first bishop, it was the most important of the new black independent churches.

cards.term: Ch. 12: What did Transcendentalism seek?
cards.def: To rise above reason through individualist spiritual communion with nature. To "transcend" meant to go beyond reason and the material world; Transcendentalists emphasized feeling and "Trust thyself."

cards.term: Ch. 12: By 1850, Catholics were what percent of the U.S. population?
cards.def: 8 percent—the same percentage as Presbyterians. The Catholic population had reached that share by 1850 after jumping to 300,000 by 1830.

cards.term: Ch. 12: What did Robert Owen teach to recruit followers?
cards.def: Shared property and equality of work division would foster tolerant people. He envisioned property held in common and work equally shared, producing tolerant, rational, self-governing people.

cards.term: Ch. 12: What happened at Seneca Falls, New York, in 1848?
cards.def: The first major women's rights convention in the United States. Stanton and Mott organized it and issued a Declaration of Sentiments: "All men and women are created equal."

cards.term: Ch. 12: Garrison's essential conviction about slavery?
cards.def: It was a sin. He urged southerners, by moral suasion, to renounce slavery as a sin—a moral question, not an economic one.

cards.term: Ch. 12: Why did the abolitionist movement split in 1840?
cards.def: Over the issue of women's rights. At the American Anti-Slavery Society convention, delegates fought over whether women could hold office; Garrison packed the meeting and his opponents walked out.

cards.term: Ch. 12: What reform effort did the gag rule temporarily defeat?
cards.def: The abolitionist drive to petition Congress against slavery. In 1836 the House automatically tabled any slavery petition; the rule was repealed in 1844.

cards.term: Ch. 12: Domesticity: father's spiritual leadership, or mother's sphere?
cards.def: Women's sphere was the home and family. The ideal did not stress the father's spiritual leadership in the home, and revivalists helped shape it rather than oppose it.

cards.term: Ch. 13: First crop planted on newly cleared cotton land?
cards.def: Corn. Farmers typically planted corn the first year after clearing, just long enough for the stumps to decompose, then switched to cotton the next spring.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Where did enslaved people outnumber white southerners by the 1850s?
cards.def: South Carolina (and also Mississippi, which is not in the choices). Elsewhere in the Deep South the black population exceeded 40 percent except in Texas; in the Upper South, whites greatly outnumbered blacks.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Why did manufacturing lag in the South?
cards.def: High profits from agriculture discouraged other possible investments. As long as cotton profits stayed high, calls for more southern industry made little headway.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Tidewater planter vs. Deep South planter?
cards.def: The Tidewater planter aspired to the ideal of the English country gentleman; the Deep South planter was an entrepreneur bound on making a fortune. Cotton gentry were typically self-made men seeking profits.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Yeoman farmers in the South...?
cards.def: Suffered from isolation, a limited market, and a chronic money shortage. They usually owned no slaves, admired rather than hated planters, and accepted slavery.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Which was NOT part of the "positive good" argument?
cards.def: That slavery's opponents could build no persuasive argument against it. Defenders did claim biblical and historical sanction, white guardianship, and that slavery was kinder than northern wage labor.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Most common form of resistance by the enslaved?
cards.def: Theft. The book calls theft the most common form of resistance and a persistent annoyance to slaveowners—garden produce, smokehouse stores, livestock, and poultry.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Significance of the Virginia debate of 1832?
cards.def: It was the last significant attempt by white southerners to take action against slavery. After Turner's revolt, the House of Delegates debated gradual emancipation, then refused 73 to 58 even to consider a bill.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Who vehemently opposed ending slavery, despite trading with the enslaved and resenting planters?
cards.def: Poor whites. They traded whiskey for stolen goods and resented planters, but opposed emancipation because Black freedom would remove one of the few symbols of their own status.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Slave revolts in North America vs. Latin America?
cards.def: In North America they were extremely rare; in Latin American slave societies, full-scale revolts were common and involved large numbers of enslaved people. The book contrasts rare U.S. revolts with frequent Latin American ones involving hundreds or thousands.

cards.term: Ch. 13: Did yeoman farmers typically own slaves?
cards.def: No. They owned no slaves, farmed about 80 to 160 acres, and made up more than half of the southern white population.
